As a representative of the constituency of Dauphin, province of Manitoba, I feel that it is my duty to offer a few remarks on the question of the extension of the boundaries

of that province, more particularly as Manitoba is probably more concerned in the matter than any other province in the Dominion. The object of the Bill is to enlarge the boundaries of Manitoba, and as to that I have no objection; the territory given to the province is perfectly satisfactory in my judgment; but I strongly oppose the handing back to Ontario of a single foot of land belonging to Manitoba.
Hear, hear.

This Bill gives to Ontario a strip of land five miles wide and 150 miles long for the purpose of building a railroad, and it also proposes to grant to Ontario a strip of land one-half mile wide and ten miles long, down the Nelson river to use as it pleases. The province of Ontario has also the privilege of taking 200 feet from Fort Nelson to Fort Churchill for the further construction of a railroad, and if they avail themselves of it, it practically gives them all the water front that is of any value on Hudson bay. For these reasons I strongly object to handing over to Ontario these valuable concessions. The strip of land to be granted to Ontario has been referred to here as the red line, but I would prefer to mark it on the map as the black line, because the fact that this territory should be given to Ontario so that it can go as it pleases through a sister province, is a black eye to Manitoba. I would want to say further that Ontario has no more right to such a grant, or to a port at Port Nelson than Manitoba has to a strip of land five miles in width to Fort William or to Port Arthur. In this respect I take the -same stand to-day that I took years ago. We were told in the province of Manitoba some years ago by the hon. Minister of the Interior, a mail for whom I have the greatest respect, and also by the Hon. Mr. Roblin, that Ontario had no right whatever to one foot of land in the territory belonging to Manitoba. On October 17th, 1905, Mr. Rogers, speaking at a party gathering in the Maw block, Winnipeg, made the following statement:
I want to say, as representing the province of Manitoba, that the province of Ontario has no more claim, as far as I understand the law and the faots as shown by the public records, than the province of British Columbia. The mere fact that Ontario lies to our east does not give her any claim either in equity or law.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Rogers cited the Privy Council judgment and the subsequent legislation by the Dominion House, and then said:
The government of Sir John Macdonald never changed a line or letter of that statement as drafted by Ontario, and yet Sir
Wilfrid Laurier, in order to further hamper, punish and discipline the province of Manitoba, undertakes to drag in the province of Ontario, which settled the boundary for itself on its own terms.
Now, Sir Wilfrid Laurier has been accused of dragging Ontario into the settlement of the boundary question. Who is guilty of dragging Ontario into the settlement of the boundary question at the present time? I say that it is not a square deal to Manitoba to make these concessions to Ontario which properly belong to Manitoba, and therefore I object to these provisions in the present Bill.
Now a word in connection with the_ swamp lands. I strongly object to handing over the swamp lands of the province of Manitoba to the Dominion. For years our local government had been demanding more swamp lands from the Dominion which was perfectly right; and now they have in the neighbourhood of seven or eight millions of acres -of these lands. These they propose now to hand back to the Dominion. I contend that as a business proposition (that is not favourable to the province of Manitoba. It is the local government's business to drain these swamp lands and bring them into condition to be cultivated, but if these lands are handed over to the Dominion, I do not believe this work will be done. We have been told by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Rogers), that he has a great immigration policy, an immigration policy that knows neither east nor west. I hope that this is true, for we want immigrants in the Dauphin district. But I would ask the minister this: when these swamp lands are handed back to the Dominion *and the work of draining them ceases, what is he going to do for his immigrants to Manitoba? It is most important to the province that these lands should be drained and settlers brought in to cultivate them. A great deal has been said about the value of swamp lands, some putting it at $3 an acre and some putting it at a higher figure. I know something about these swamp lands, and I know that when drained they are the most productive lands we have. That has been proven beyond a doubt, especially in my district where we have a considerable area of these swamp lands. For these reasons, I object to these lands being handed back to the Dominion. We are told that the government will hand these lands back again to Manitoba at some future day. That may be true or it may not be true. We were told by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) when he appeared in the western country that if he were returned to power he would net give the people of Canada reciprocity. He was admired by the western people
(COMMONS
for his courage in making that statement. But he went further and stated that if returned to power he would carry out the Farmers' Bill of rights to the letter and would give them government ownership and control of elevators. Where do we find him to-day? The people took him at his word, but he has not delivered the goods and given us government ownership and control of . elevators. How do we know, then, that he will hand back these lands to Manitoba?. It seems to me that this is nothing better than a hold-up. The lands, we are told, will be handed back to the province at a future date. But when? At the next general election? In that case, what will be the argument? It will be: If you vote for the Conservative party you will get your lands back? That is not a square deal. And for that reason I object to it. I support the interests of the province of Manitoba, where I lived for many years and hope to live for a good many yet. These are my reasons for objecting to certain clauses in this Boundary Bill.

I desire to speak on the general question, but more particularly with respect to the amendment of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr Oliver). I have no objection to the boundaries of [DOT]Manitoba being extended. There has been a general desire on the part of the people of Manitoba for a number of years for an extension of the boundaries of their province. But there has also been a general desire on the part of the people of Saskatchewan for an extension of the boundaries of their province toward Hudson bay. As to that, I hope to speak more directly before I conclude, but, in the meantime I wish to offer a few observations with regard to the financial terms under this Bill. Hon. members who take the trouble to go back to the debate of 1905 and read the speeches of men who were then in opposition, and are now on the treasury benches, will be apt to wonder how these gentlemen who opposed the financial terms given to Saskatchewan and Alberta can to-day support the terms being given to Manitoba, particularly as the government say that the object of the Bill is to place Manitoba on the same footing, financially and otherwise, as these other provinces. One of these speeches was by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster). He criticised the late government for the financial terms that were being given to Saskatchewan and Alberta, and said practically that these provinces were getting too much.
No, he did not.

He said to the government: This measure wall bring down upon the government every province of the Mr. CRUISE.
Dominion; already I hear the rumbling of discontent among the western provinces; and he went on to say that he hoped the Minister of Finance, before he pressed the Bill forward, would revise the financial considerations about to be given to the new provinces. And now we are told by the leader of the government (Mr. Borden) that Manitoba is being placed on exactly the same footing as Saskatchewan and Alberta. How can the Minister of Trade and commerce (Mr. Poster), in view of his statement then with regard to Alberta and Saskatchewan, support to-day the terms being given to Manitoba under this Bill ?
It makes the provinces equal.

But the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) said that the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta were being given too much; today he says the province of Manitoba is being given just enough; and yet, according to the Prime Minister and other hon. gentlemen opposite, the province of Manitoba is being given exactly what these other provinces were given. I do not say that the treatment of the provinces is equal. I had here beside me a copy of volume 2 of ' Hansard ' of 1905 containing a speech by the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk). I am'sorry that it has been taken away, for it deprives me of the opportunity to quote the hon. gentleman's exact words. But it was practically the same line of argument. He said there was no reason why Quebec should be called upon to assist in paying these immense subsidies to Alberta and Saskatchewan. But, to-day he is prepared to support the same terms when given to Manitoba. I do not wish to be understood as finding fault with Manitoba getting a square deal. If the Manitoba members are satisfied with this Bill, all right. If I were a member from Manitoba, I should not be satisfied with it. But there are certain features of this Bill which show discrimination in favour of Manitoba against Saskatchewan and Alberta. One of these was well stated by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). According to the Bill, Manitoba obtains a debt allowance on a population of 250,000, the same, I believe, as the debt allowance that was given to Saskatchewan and Alberta.
To-day in the province of Saskatchewan we have a population of something like 495,000, while the province of Manitoba has 455,000; we have 40,000 more than Manitoba. Therefore, in order to place Saskatchewan on the same footing as Manitoba we should have in Saskatchewan an increased debt allowance based on our
40,000	additional population, which would mean a debt allowance of

$1,280,000. That is one of the discriminations in favour of Manitoba against Saskatchewan and Alberta. There is another point. The population in Manitoba is confined to a comparatively small area. If .you draw a line diagonally from the southeast corner of Manitoba to the northwest [DOT]and take the country south of that, you will find an area of 40,000 square miles of inhabited country. In the province of Saskatchewan only the southern half is well populated, covering an area of about
125.000	square miles. It is not so expensive to administer the province of Manitoba as it is to administer the province of Saskatchewan. In Manitoba to-day roads, bridges and schools must be provided for over an area of about 40,000 square miles, while in Saskatchewan roads, bridges and schools must be provided for over an area of 125,000 square miles. It is therefore less expensive to administer the province of Manitoba than the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. So this constitutes another discrimination in favour of Manitoba.
There is another matter. The province of Manitoba secured 150,000 acres of selected lands for university purposes. Saskatchewan never secured any land for such a purpose neither has Alberta. The 150,000 acres of university lands selected in Manitoba are being written off, according to this measure, at $2 per acre. I would like, as a representative from Saskatchewan, to he allowed to select 150,000 acres of land in that province for university purposes at $2 per acre. I say that this government, in [DOT]order to place Saskatchewan and Alberta on an equal footing with Manitoba in this Tespect, must give us the right to select
150.000	acres of land for university purposes in each one of those provinces.
Now the. question of arrearages has been referred to. I do not profess to be able to throw any new light on the subject, and will only present it to you as it appears to me. as a representative of Saskatchewan. After looking over the speeches that have been delivered by the Prime Minister and other hon. gentlemen of the opposition dealing with the payment of arrearages io the province of Manitoba, I confess that I have not been able to find any justification for it. What do they say? That as early as 1905, when Manitoba wanted to have her boundaries increased and her territories extended to Hudson Bay, the Prime Minister says he could not admit her contention that they should date back to 1009. When the resolution was passed by the late government extending the boundaries to Hudson bay, it appears, if I am correctly informed, that the Manitoba government never accepted those boundaries until the month of March, 1911, and never formally notified the government of Canada of their acceptance until the month of March 1911. To my mind the Manitoba
government have not got a solitary leg to stand upon in respect to the pavment of arrearages. I do not wish to cast any reflections upon the present government of Manitoba. The Minister of the Interior a few days ago ventured to say that_ the finances of the province of Manitoba were in the best position, in as good a position as those of any other province in Canada. I do not know anything about the position of the finances of the province of Manitoba; I do know', however, that on their telephone transaction, when they purchased the telephones throughout the province and operated them as a government concern for the past three or four years, they are something like $450,000 behind at the present time in the operation of that system. I also know that they have lost money in the operation of their government-owned elevators. I do not need to go outside the province of Manitoba to get information of her finances. About six weeks ago when I was in Winnipeg, I was told many times that the government	of Manitoba	were	financiallyin a very bad position. I can only say	that it is my	belief	that	thissum	of	$2,178,000 to	be handed	overto Manitoba in payment of arrearages	is	merely being	given	as a	sop
to that province, and as a rope to pull her out of a hole. I do believe that were it not for the financial assistance which the Manitoba government expects to get out of this payment of arrearages, they would not have a ghost of a chance in the next election.
Because the old legislature of the North-w'est Territories, as far as they are covered the province of Saskatchewan, passed a resolution to the effect that the time had come when a province should be formed, we might just as well argue, that the payments under the autonomy legislation of 1905 should date back to 1902 as hon. gentlemen can argue that Manitoba's arrearages should date back to 1908 as provided in this Bill. Let me further point out to emphasize my argument that pursuant to the resolution passed in the territorial legislature in 1902 Mr. Haultain drew up a draft Bill which he submitted to the late government as a basis on which the two provinces should be caivect out of the Northwest Territories. With just as good reason, therefore, you might argue that Alberta and Saskatchewan should receive financial consideration back to 1902, as you can argue that Manitoba should be paid arrearages amounting to $2,178,000 dating back to 1908. In my opinion this is an outrage to the rest of the people of Canada, and a further discrimination in favour of Manitoba as against the other two provinces.
There is another matter that occurs to me in connection with this Bill, and that

is the question of our natural resources. Ever since the year 1905, in -western Canada, every Conservative candidate always promised, not only in Manitoba but in Saskatchewan and Alberta, that immediately the Conservative party came into power it would restore our natural resources to those three provinces. Now here is an opportunity for the present Conservative government to fulfil their promises and show their good faith. Here is an opportunity for the Prime Minister to fulfil the promises which he made when he was touring western Canada last summer, when he toid them he was in favour of restoring the natural resources to those provinces. No further legislation is required, here is an opportunity for him to do it. Let me refer to one or two statements that were made by the present Prime Minister in the west last year. First of all, let me read the statement that was made by the right hon. gentleman at Halifax on August 21, 1907-I believe it has already been quoted in this House. The hon. gentleman said:
In 1905 the Conservatives took the position that under our constitution the public domain within each province ought to he committed to the management and administration of the people of that province through their provincial governments. That was the basis of arrangement between the four provinces originally constituting the Dominion. At the present time every province in Canada controls and administers its public lands except 'the three provinces of Manitoba Saskatchewan and Alberta.
He concluded as follows:
We have not receded from the policy which we announced two years ago, and therefore we are prepared to restore their public lands to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan upon fair terms.
The platform of the Conservative party circulated in western Canada during the recent election contained this paragraph about handing over their natural resources to the prairie provinces. That was the main argument of the Conservative party in my constituency, [DOT] granting the natural resources to the prairie provinces. Then at Winnipeg, in 1911, when the right hon. gentleman was dealing with this question, he said:
Before discussing a subject of great publio interest now under the consideration of parliament, I desire to touch upon certain questions of paramount importance to the people of the west. To-day in Canada six provinces enjoy the right to control and administer the public lands, mines, minerals and other natural resources within their boundaries. That right is not enjoyed by the three prairie provinces. The Liberal-Conservative party since 1902 has firmly asserted and maintained the rights of these three provinces to their public domain. We stand for that right to-day and we will maintain it. The public lands, and

natural resources are vested in the Crown, to be administered for the benefit of the people. In six provinces the Crown, in dealing with the public domain acts upon the advice of the provincial ministers and under laws enacted by the provincial legislatures. In the three prairie provinces the Crown in dealing with such lands acts upon the advice of the federal ministers and under laws enacted by the federal parliament. Why should there he any such discrimination against the people of these three provinces? The day is not far distant when Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta will receive from a Liberal-Conservative government at Ottawa the just recognition of their undoubted right to their public lands and natural resources.
There is a Liberal-Conservative government at Ottawa at the present time; why does not that Liberal-Conservative government implement its promise, particularly to the province of Manitoba, and give these natural resources to that province? That was a speech made by the right hon. gentleman at Winnipeg. But I have here an extract from a speech made by the Prime Minister at Brandon in the month of July, 1911. He said:
In 1902, dn 1905, in 1907, and again in 1910, we have stood for the right of the western provinces to own and control their public domain. It is the right of the people of th ose provinces to have their public lands and natural resources administered by their own governments under the control of their own legislatures. They say that they are free men and being free men in a free country have as good a right to control through their owu 'local legislatures, and by their own provincial executives, the administration of their publio lands and natural resources as have the people of any of the eastern provinces who enjoy and have enjoyed that right. The Liberal-Conservative party supports that claim and will enforce dt at the first opportunity.
As far as the province of Manitoba is concerned here is an opportunity; yet, the promise which was made at Winnipeg and Brandon during last summer has not been implemented. Not only have we the promise of the right hon. Prime Minister, but other members of the present administration have expressed themselves very strongly with respect to the control of the natural resources of the prairie provinces.
I have to go no farther than to the hon. Secretary-of State (Mr. Roche) who discussed this subject in the House of Commons in 1906, and, if I remember correctly, he made similar remarks in speaking at Regina, when I had the pleasure of hearing him. I may tell the Secretary of State that he did not do me very much harm when he was in Regina. Speaking on the question of the coal strike in 1906, on a resolution moved by the then member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) the hon. Secretary of State said:

The hon. member for Qu'Appolle (Mr. Lake) lias spoken about the humiliating position in which our country has been placed. In the first place I claim it was a humiliating position in which to place those new provinces to withold from their hands .the control of their own public lands. Had the rights of the people of those provinces been fought for as they should have been fought for by hon. gentlemen supporting the government, the provinces would have control over their lands to-day, and the provinces would have been able to grapple with their own coal strike without calling on the federal government for relief.
If that was a humiliating position for the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta to be placed in then, I submit it is a much more humiliating position for the province of Manitoba to be placed in to-day in view of the assurances that were given not only by the right hon. the Prime Minister, but by other ministers and by every Conservative candidate throughout the west during many years past. Hon. members from Manitoba told us in 1905 that Alberta and Saskatchewan were being placed in a most humiliating position. Why do they not rise to the occasion now and help us to keep Manitoba from being placed in such a humiliating position and from being deprived of the management of her natural resources and lands?
Then, there is this question of the swamp lands to which I want to allude for a minute. There have been various estimates made of the value of these swamp lands which were handed over to Manitoba under the Act which was passed in 1885. I believe that it is estimated that something like 8,000,000 acres of swamp lands still belong to Manitoba. The estimate made by the provincial treasurer of Manitoba, Mr. Armstrong, was that these lands were worth something like $16,000,000. My hon. friend from Edmonton has stated that this sum, capitalized at 5 per cent, would produce $800,000 per annum and, according to the calculation of my hon. friend from Edmonton, Manitoba would be in a far better financial position to keep these lands, even provided they produced only $3 per acre, and get $800,000 per annum than to accept the terms proposed by the Bill now before the committee. I submit that $3 per acre is not a sufficient value for these swamp lands. If the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury), who used to wax eloquent in connection with St. Peter's Indian reserve, were in the House, I would call him as a witness. He used to estimate that these reserve swamp lands were worth from $25 to $30 per acre.
The hon. membei from Selkirk is in the House. I would like to correct the hon. gentleman.
Just as soon &f I get through the hon. gentleman may follow me.
What the hon. gentleman has stated is absolutely incorrect.

I have not any doubt at all that 'Hansard' will prove that what I have stated is absolutely correct, that the hon. member for Selkirk did estimate the lands of St. Peter's Indian reserve to be worth from $25 to $30 per acre.
I beg to say that the hon. gentleman is .absolutely incorrect. There are not more than 8,000 acres of swamp land out of the whole 40,000 acres contained within St. Peter's Indian reserve

I am forced to accept the hon. gentleman's statement. However, it is a matter of small import in any event. I submit that $3 per acre for the swamp lands in Manitoba is a very small valuation. I believe that these lands are worth at least $10 per acre. Take 8,000,000 acres at $10 per acre and you have $80,000,000 and therefore the argument presented by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) that the terms offered bv the recent administration, according to which Manitoba was to retain her swamp lands and get a grant of $200,000 per annum in lieu of the balance of land not granted, was a better proposition for Manitoba than the terms submitted by the present government, is quite correct.
Then, before I conclude my remarks, I wish to direct the attention of the commitee to a matter which is of great importance to the province of Saskatchewan and to refer to the rights of that province to have some consideration in connection with a port on Hudson Bay. If you go back to the question of what territory is involved in the territory that is being added to Manitoba you will find that it is made up of parts of the original territories of Saskatchewan and Athabasca, Keewatin and the territory which lies between Ontario and Hudson Bay. There are only three provinces which can possibly be interested in that territory and they are Ontario, to the east, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. The province of Saskatchewan, as early as the year 1906 or 1907, put forward a claim for an extension of her boundaries to a port on the bay. I submit that in deciding the question you must of necessity go into the history of these territories, and that, in as far as that portion of Athabasca and of the old district of Saskatchewan which is being added to Manitoba are concerned, the province which has the paramount and absolute interest is Saskatchewan. When the province of Saskatchewan was formed there were parts of the old district of Athabasca and the old district of Saskatchewan that were not included.
Those districts and those parts of those districts which are now being put into Manitoba, were formerly part of the old

Northwest Territories and were administered by the government of the old Northwest Territories. The school law of the old Northwest Territories which was in force until 1905 was in force in those parts of Athabasca and Saskatchewan district which are now being added to the province of Manitoba. Those parts of those districts, as a matter of fact, were represented in the old territorial legislature of the Northwest Territories, now represented by the legislature of Saskatchewan and the legislature of Alberta. The -old government of the Northwest Territories was responsible for the construction of roads and bridges, and schools in those territories, and, as I have said, those parts of Athabasca and Saskatchewan were represented in the legislature by Mr. Samuel McLeod. Formerly, I believe, they constituted part of what was known as the district of Cumberland, and latterly the district of East Prince Albert. As a matter of fact these portions of territory were represented in this House of Commons in the old district of Mackenzie by a gentleman who still occupies a seat in this House. This territory which is being added to the province of Manitoba, was just as much a part of the old Northwest Territorities as the city of Regina, or the town of Indian Head, or any other municipality located in the central part of that province. In addition to the fact that the province of Saskatchewan has a paramount and absolute interest beyond any other province, in the part of this territory which has been referred to-the part that lies north of the Nelson river and between the Nelson river and Hudson bay-in addition to that I submit that in apportioning the territories among the three provinces, it is generally admitted that each of these provinces was entitled to have access to Hudson bay. If you will look at the map I think every one will agree that the province of Saskatchewan, beyond any other province in the Dominion, is entitled to access to a port on Hudson bay. Our province is the most vitally interested in the construction of the Hudson Bay railway. I submit that it is beyond dispute that the province of Saskatchewan will use that Hudson Bay railway for transportation facilities far more than will any of the other provinces of the Dominion. I believe than any railroad that is constructed out of Saskatchewan or Manitoba towards Hudson ' bay, will be used by Saskatchewan more than it will be used by Manitoba. The products of Saskatchewan are to-day greater in volume than are the products of Manitoba, and there will be greater disparity between the two provinces in this respect in years to come, so that of necessity any railway that is constructed towards Hudson bay will be more used1 by the people of Saskatchewan than by the people of Manitoba or of Mr. MARTIN (Regina).
Ontario. I submit that Saskatchewan would only be getting a square deal if it were given access to Hudson bay, and given the same consideration at least as the province of Ontario is getting.
There are further facts to consider in connection with this matter. As far as any evidence I have been able to find goes, the inhabitants of the territory which is being annexed have never themselves evinced any desire to be annexed to Manitoba, but, on the contrary, they have evinced a desire to be annexed' to Saskatchewan. I find in volume 1 of the Sessional Papers of 1906-07, (hat when the legislation of 1905 was under consideration in this House, the people of that part of Athabasca and Saskatchewan petitioned to be included in Saskatchewan, and I shall read a short extract from a petition which the people of these territories forwarded to the Prime Minister at that time:
We, the undersigned electors of Mackenzie district, Northwest Territories, and residing at or near the Pas, Saskatchewan, having learned but recently that an effort is being made by the government of Manitoba to have that portion of the territories, lying north of Manitoba, joined to and inoluded in the province of Manitoba, and such annexation being repugnant to us, and as we believe detrimental to the best interests of this portion of the country, we therefore humbly petition that our political affiliation may be with the territories and not with Manitoba, and in case of provincial autonomy being granted the territories, our destiny may be in and with that portion of the territories of which we form an integral part and for such, as in duty hound, your petitioners will ever pray.
Therefore, we have the inhabitants of this territory petitioning not to be annexed to Manitoba, and so far as I have learned, there is not on record any petition to the contrary.
. The territory which I submit Saskatchewan is entitled to, is as follows:
The territory bounded on the south by the province of Manitoba; on the west by the province of Saskatchewan; on the north by the thirty-second correction line of the Dominion lands townships system of survey, which is very nearly the sixtieth parallel of north latitude; on the east by a line commencing at the point where the 100th meridian of west longitude intersects the thirty-second correction line aforesaid, thence following the said 100th meridian south to the eighteenth correction line in the said system of survey, than'-e in an easterly direction along the said eighteenth correction line to a point where the said correction line intersects the Nelson river, thence southerly along the Nelson river to Lake Winnipeg, thence along the northern and western shores of Lake Winnipeg in a southerly direction to the point where it intersects the northern boundary of the province of Manitoba.
I presume that in view of the position taken by the government, and in view of
469/

the fact that the Bill is submitted to us, there is very little use of my urging that the province of Saskatchewan should be given that territory. I present this view, however, as the view taken by the vast majority of the people of the province of Saskatchewan. However, I do submit that if the government desire to render Saskatchewan justice, or if it wants to render Saskatchewan as much justice as it is rendering to the province of Ontario, it should at least do for Saskatchewan that which it proposes to do for Ontario. I will read, so that it may be on record, a telegram which Avas recently sent by the Acting Premier of Saskatchewan to the Rt. Hon. R. L. Borden, Prime Minister:
Regina, March 6.

Borden,
Premier of Canada. Ottawa, Ont
The government of Saskatchewan understands that legislation now before parliament contains provision whereby the province of Ontario will have the rights to secure access to Ports Nelson and Churchill on Hudson bay. Ou behalf of the people of Saskatchewan we deem it our duty to again call your attention to the claims of this province as set forth in the memorial now in your hands. We desire to protest in the strongest manner possible against the provision of the Bill now before parliament which ignores the just claims of Saskatchewan for access to the bay. We wish further to point out that if there is a [DOT]single valid reason why the province of Ontario should be given access to the ports mentioned, there are many reasons which are made apparent in the memorial referred to why Saskatchewan should have its claims recognized.
In view of the fact that you did not grant the request of the government of Saskatchewan to be represented at the conferences held with the governments of Manitoba and Ontario we *desire to take this means, the only course open to us at present, to notify the government of Canada on behalf of our people that if the legislation now before parliament regarding an extension of the boundaries of Manitoba and Ontario become law without proper provision being made therein for a recognition, not of the claims, but of the rights of this province, the citizens of Saskatchewan for all time to come will have just cause to complain of the treatment received by them. In dealing with the matter referred to, our people have the right to hope and expect that your government will be guided by principles of justice and equality, thereby ensuring that the various provinces in the confederation of -Canada will have no cause to complain of unfair treatment.
Will my hon. friend read *the reply to that?

I will do so. The position taken by the Saskatchewan government is mainly that that province is entitled to the territory outlined in the record which I have read from the sessional papers of 1907. But they also claim as au alternative that if the government of Canada do not see their way to give Saskatchewan any portion of that territory, with a port on Hudson Bay, that province should have at least the same consideration as has been given to the province of Ontario in the order in council recently passed. In asking for this, we are not asking for very much; for 1 think the present government, to use a common expression, has. handed the province of Ontario a lemon. They have given it what is of no use to it. It does not own the land; it gets a simple right of way through the territory of Manitoba. This is simply handed out to the province of Ontario to hoodwink the people of that province. So that in giving the same kind of consideration to the people of Saskatchewan, I do cot think the Dominion government would be giving us much. I think they should give us a great deal more to meet the need of the province for an outlet to Hudson Bay. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) asked me to read the reply which has been .sent by the right hon. the Prime Minister to the government of Saskatchewan. That reply is as follows:-
I beg to acknowledge your telegram of yesterday. The legislation now before parliament does not contain the provision alluded to. The province of Ontario considers it desirable to extend its state-owned railway to a port on Hudson bay.
At this point I would say that the present government has no guarantee from the government of Ontario that they are going to extend that railway to Hudson bay. All that the order in council says is that it might be desirable in the interest of the province to extend the railway to Hudson bay. I can say exactly the same on behalf of the province of Saskatchewan. Although we have no state-owned railway, it might be desirable in the interest of the province to have a state-owned railway running to Hudson bay. This is just as much assurance as the government has xe-ceived from the - government of Ontario. There is no agreement on the part of the province of Ontario to extend the railway. As I am not through, Mr. Chairman, will you call it six o'clock.

speechtext:
I understood that the discussion was to be concluded by six o'clock; at least that was the intimation
conveyed to me.

There was no agreement, but it was said that we would not interpose any obstacle to having it concluded by six o'clock.
At six o'clock, House took recess.

After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL.

speechtext:
House in committee on Bill (No. 30) respecting the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Co.-Mr. White (Renfrew).
On section 1-time for construction extended,

subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL.
speechtext: This Bill has been the subject of considerable criticism, and perhaps the hon. gentleman in charge of it would inform the committee what is the present position of affairs.

subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL.
speechtext: The Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Bill was partly considered in committee, and then referred to a subcommittee. The subcommittee met the representatives of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and discussed the measure, and amended it to some extent. It was reprinted as amended by the subcommittee, and then came back to the Standing Committee on Railways. It was considered by them as reprinted, and it was adopted without any further objection. The main features that were in discussion were to have it defined clearly who should be the directors. It was proposed that the survivors of those that were originally directors should be the directors of the company. Now it is held that certain persons shall be the directors. The other proposition which gave rise to the most difficulty was, as to the right to take property belonging to the provinces without the provinces having anything to say in regard to that. It is now provided that, except for the purposes of the canal construction, the company shall not take any land without the consent of the province of Quebec, or the province of Ontario, as the case may be. Then I think there was a provision changed submitting to the jurisdiction of the Railway Board, and they have the Bill before them. I think those were the changes that were made.

subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL.
speechtext: I am not very familiar with the case, but I have seen some criticism of this Bill based, I think, on the ground that it may be used as a foundation of claim against the government of Canada, in case it was decided to go on with the construction of the Georgian Bay canal as a government work. If the railway company and the House at large are satisfied with that position I am not going to raise any objection, only I would like to have that point brought out so

subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL.
speechtext: that it might be seen that we are not passing the Bill absolutely in the dark.

speechtext: I think I can satisfy the House and the hon. member as to that point. When the committee rose at six o'clock, I was endeavouring to deal with the reply which was sent by the Prime Minister to the request received by this government from the government of the province of Saskatchewan for increased territory, or for at least similar treatment to that accorded the province of Ontario. For the purpose of placing the telegram completely before the House, I will read it:
I beg to acknowledge your telegram of yesterday. The legislation now before parliament does not contain the provision alluded to. The province of Ontario considers it desirable to extend its state-owned railway to a port on Hudson bay. For this purpose the Governor in Council has passed an order granting to that province a strip of land five miles in width from the western boundary of Ontario to the mouth of the Nelson river. This grant is made by virtue of the federal ownership of the land within the extended boundaries of Manitoba. In ease the pr ov-ince of Saskatchewan should undertake the construction and operation of a state owned railway to the shores of Hudson bay, this government will be glad to give the proposal the most careful and earnest c onsideration. May I point out, however, that apart from this the claim of Saskatchewan was disposed of by the late administration on the 13th July, 1908; Sir Wilfrid Laurier expressed the decision of his government in the following
words; ' After giving due consideration to this olaim on the part of the province of Saskatchewan, it seemed to us that, as between the claim of the province of Saskatchewan and the province of Manitoba, to have the new territory which lies north of Manitoba and east of Saskatchewan alloted either one way or the other the weight of argument was certainly in favour of Manitoba, and we could not grant the prayer of Saskatchewan. We therefore had to ignore it.
There are two or three points in this reply to which I wish to call attention. The first one I mentioned before six o'clock, the words ' the province of Ontario thinks it desirable to extend its state-owned railway to a port in Hudson bay.' Now, I submit that that statement is not borne out by the order in council passed by the government giving certain rights to Ontario in the shape of a strip of land to a port on the Hudson bay. All the order in council says is as follows:
The government of the province of Ontario considers that it would or might be desirable in the interest of the province to extend the provincial railway known as the Timiskaming and Northern railway

All that the order in council says is that it ' would or might be desirable '. The telegram says that the government of the province of Ontario considers it desirable. We have no evidence, and the government has no evidence and I do not believe that this road is going to be extended by the province of Ontario. I submit that in order to carry out the effect of that telegram word for word there should be some agreement between the government of the province of Ontario whereby it undertakes to build that railroad from Hudson bay, otherwise the whole contention of the right hon. gentleman in this telegram falls to the gronnd. Furtherfore, what does he say to the province of Saskatchewan;
In case the province of Saskatchewan should undertake the construction and operation

The right hon. gentleman did not ask from the province of Ontario an undertaking to construct that Timiskaming road to Hudson bay, but he is asking from the province of Saskatchewan, before we can get similar consideration an actual undertaking to build a state-owned road from some point in that province to Hudson bay. But he does not say in the telegram that we will get the same treatment as the province of Ontario, even if we undertake to construct a road, but he simply says if such be the case this government will be glad to give the proposals the most careful and earnest consideration. The most the province of Saskatchewan can expect if she does undertake to build a state-owned railway from some point in that province to Hudson bay, is ' careful and earnest consideration '. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, to compare that treatment accorded to us with

the treatment accorded to Ontario. The province of Ontario was never asked for any undertaking, they got this consideration without any undertaking whatever.
Some hon. gentlemen will say that the late government disposed of this whole question. It is true the late government disposed of the question so far as the territory was concerned. But I point out that the late government did not concede the demands of the province of Ontario, and the present government has re-opened the whole question by giving to Ontario a certain strip of land and a certain right to a port on the Hudson bay. The late government did not concede that, therefore the present government have re-opened, the whole question, and I say that in all fairness we are entitled to equal consideration with the province of Ontario. Hon. gentlemen opposite are very glad, and very anxious, to shelter themselves behind the decisions of the late government, and I do not blame them for it. The decisions of the late government were usually correct. But in this case the present government are sheltering themselves behind the decision of the late government in regard to Saskatchewan, but they do not shelter themselves behind the decision of the late government in regard to Ontario. Now I fancy that not many men sitting here from the province of Ontario believe that the Ontario government is going to construct the Timiskaming railway to Hudson bay. It does not seem to me to be reasonable that the Ontario government is going to extend that Timiskaming railway to Hudson bay, or from Cochrane to Hudson bay. It appears to me more reasonable that they might extend it to the city of Quebec, and especially in view of the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite to keep the trade of this country running east and west. The distance from Cochrane to the city of Quebec is 475 miles, the distance from Cochrane to Ste. Margaret's bay, the nearest point on the Hudson bay, is 625 miles. The distance from Cochrane to Port Nelson terminus on Hudson bay is 700 miles. Now the common sense view of the matter appears to me to be that this Timiskaming railway from Cochrane will in all probability be extended to the city of Quebec.
I said before the committee rose at six o clock that the province of Saskatchewan had more interest in transportation to Hudson bay than any other province in the Dominion of Canada. I do not require to elaborate that statement. But let me give you one or two figures to indicate that we are really more interested, because of our nearness to ports on the Hudson bay, in the traffic that may be conducted with any port, or through any railroad connected with that bay, than Mr. MARTIN (Regina*
even the province of Manitoba. Take the distance from the centre of these provinces. The centre of Manitoba is very much closer to Fort William than the-centre of Saskatchewan. From the centre of Manitoba to Fort William is a distance of about 500 miles. From the centre of Saskatchewan. to Fort William is a distance of 800 miles. But from the centre of Saskatchewan to Churchill is a distance of 500 to 550 miles; whereas, the distance from the centre of Manitoba to Fort Churchill is some 750 to 800 miles by the nearest route. The centre of Saskatchewan is far nearer than the centre of Manitoba to either one of these ports on the bay. Therefore, I say we are more interested in transportation to Hudson bay than the province of Manitoba can be. Let me conclude my remark by giving a brief resume of the reasons I have given for the contention that we are entitled to added territory, but in any event we are entitled to equal consideration with the province of Ontario:
1.	Those parts of old districts of Saskatchewan and Athabaska not included in the province of Saskatchewan were for 20 years, and should continue to be, united with the area forming that province.
2.	The province of Saskatchewan and the province of Manitoba are both entitled to have their boundaries extended to Hudson bay.
3.	By granting to the province of Saskatchewan those portions of the old districts of Saskatchewan and Athabaska, the Nelson river forms a natural boundary, and I submit, a reasonable boundary between that province and Manitoba.
4.	The territory north of the Nelson river is tributary to the province of Saskatchewan rather than to Manitoba.
5.	The province of Saskatchewan has a much greater interest in a transportation route via Hudson bay to the European market than has either Manitoba or Ontario.
6.	If the territory north of Wilson river were given to Saskatchewan, no great injustice would be done to Manitoba because there would still be left 208,000 square miles of equally good territory with several hundred miles of coast line, which is amply sufficient to satisfy all reasonable claims both of Manitoba and Ontario.
I submit that in order to do even scant justice to the province of Saskatchewan we must be accorded like treatment with the province of Ontario. That statement cannot be successfully refuted. I have only this to say to the present government, that if they do not give the province of Saskatchewan access to a port on the Hudson bay in the same way as they do to the province of Ontario, the people of Saskatchewan will have a just cause for com-

plaint, and a just grievance against this government for all time to come.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would like to say one or two words in reply to the observations of my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Martin). He will pardon me if I do not advert to the major portion of his speech, because it simply contains arguments that have been made a great many times in the discussion of this measure, and which 1 think have been answered a great many times. But with reference to the alleged discrimination Detween Ontario and Saskatchewan, I want to point out that the word ' undertaking ' was not used in the telegram in the sense which he attributes to it. It was used in the sense of embarking upon the project of building a railroad to Hudson bay, it was not used in the sense of requiring any undertaking from the province of Saskatchewan, and I regret that my hon. friend took that meaning from it. I may be permitted to say that inasmuch as he regards the arrangement with Ontario as either a lemon or a gold brick, I am not sure which, I am surprised that he should be exercised so greatly in order to get a similar lemon or gold brick for the province of Saskatchewan. He is of course entitled to his own opinion as to the character of the particular arrangement that has been made. If he still should be anxious for this alleged lemon or gold brick, as the hon. member has called it, for the province of Saskatchewan, I have already said in the telegram that the government would be desirous of giving its most earnest and careful consideration to any proposal that the province of Saskatchewan might make in that regard.
In so far as the desire of the province of Ontario is concerned, I do not recollect at the moment the exact words that were used in the order in council, but I do know that the government of Ontario, in so far as I can gather the intentions of that government, has it in most serious contemplation to extend the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway to a port on Hudson bay. My hon. friend is a little astray, I think, in one regard. In so far as the boundaries are concerned, they are left exactly as they were defined in 1908. The arrangement made with the province of Ontario is not a part of this legislation. If legislation is hereafter to be placed before this House for the purpose of carrying out that arrangement made with Ontario, my hon. friend's observations will be very much more' to the'point than they have been this afternoon and evening, although I concede, of course, that he is at perfect liberty and quite within his rights in making the comments upon the arrangement that he has seen fit to make.
I do not think that my hon. friend was a member of this House in 1908 when the resolutions were moved on the 13th of July, and therefore 1 cannot ask him why he kept silent on that occasion because he was not here to say anything for the province of Saskatchewan. Perhaps I am mistaken in that.
He was here.
I was not here in 1908.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is my recollection. But, I would like to say to him that Saskatchewan was represented by capable and zealous men at that time, and I do not remember-I am speaking from recollection-that any member from Saskatchewan then found fault with the attitude of the late administration on that occasion. My hon. friend suggests that the present administration is desirous of hiding itself behind the late administration. We are not so desirous. The (present government thought that the boundaries which were defined by this House in 1908 ought to be adhered to and, consistently with that, we thought it no more than right to give some effective consideration to the desire and claim of the province of Ontario to extend its state-owned railway to the shore of Hudson bay. In doing that we have not departed at all from the boundaries. We have simply, by the exercise of the rights appertaining to the government of this country in virtue of the federal ownership of these lands within the extended boundaries, given this strip of land to the province of Ontario in order that it may have an opportunity of extending that railway to the shore of Hudson bay. If the province of Saskatchewan should desire to enter into the project of owning and operating railways, and should desire to extend its railways to the shore of Hudson bay, I can only repeat to my hon. friend what I have already said to the government of Saskatchewan in the telegram which has been brought up, that this government will be prepared to give the most earnest and sympathetic consideration to any suggestions or proposals that the government of Saskatchewan may have to make in regard to the matter.'
. Mr. MARTIN (Regina). Could that be done in any way at all after this Bill extending the boundaries of Manitoba has passed?
Mr. BORDEN, I am afraid that I have not made myself clear to my hon. friend. I trust that I have made myself clearer to most hon. gentlemen in this House than I seem to have succeeded in doing in so far as he is concerned. The boundaries are

adhered to exactly as they were before, but inasmuch as the Crown, in the right of the government of Canada, owns the greater part of the land within the extended boundaries, the government of Canada could make a grant for railway purposes to a 'Corporation, or an individual, or to any one else. This is not strictly connected with the extension of the boundaries. If the boundaries of Manitoba had not been extended at all it would' have been equally competent for the government of Canada to have made a grant to that province for the purpose referred to. The two things are not directly connected with each other, except in so far as they are connected in this way: Ontario made a claim that it was entitled to have a port on the shores of Hudson bay, but the boundaries having been defined by parliament in 1908, it seemed that the best course open to us for the purpose, was to make a grant of this strip five miles in width in order that it might be competent for the province of Ontario to extend that railway through the province of Manitoba just as it could have extended that railway through these territories before they formed a part of the province of Manitoba. I am putting aside for the moment, the alleged constitutional difficulties which have been raised by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House and to which I do not attach a great deal of importance. But, that is all that has been done. If the boundaries had not been extended the same thing might have been done, or if the boundaries of Manitoba were extended to-day and Ontario, three years from now, had come to the conclusion that it desired to extend its railway to the shores of Hudson bay, it would have been competent for this government at that time, to have done exactly the same thing. It is only in the way i have suggested, that the two proposals are connected with each other.

When the boundaries of Manitoba were definitely settled in 1908, the same resolution dealt with the boundaries of Ontario and Quebec, whereas in the present case, the government is dealing with the boundaries of each of these provinces by a separate Bill. In 1908 a resolution was moved by the hon. member for Colchester to the following effect:
Be it resolved 'that the extension of the boundaries provided for by this resolution shall he accompanied by such conditions as will prevent such extension prejudicially affecting the representation of any province in parliament.
An amendment was moved to that resolution. which was adopted, I think, by consent, as follows:
That in any legislation to he introduced to give effect to the foregoing resolution, nothing shall be contained or provided to impair the representation of any province in this House.

In view of this, I call the attention of the Prime Minister to the effect of the extension of provincial boundaries upon the representation of the provinces in parliament. The Prime Minister, coming from the maritime provinces, is aware of the interest which has developed in that portion of the Dominion in regard to this question of representation. In the organ of his party in the Island of Cape Breton, it was urged that the members of this House, irrespective of party, should, in connection with this Bill, take up this question of representation, and have it settled. During the discussion in 1908, the hon. member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler), and the then member from St. John county (Dr. Daniel), dealt at great length with that question, and the effect which the extension of these boundaries would have upon the question of representation. I do not propose to move an amendment, but I want to say a word or two to the right hon. gentleman in regard to this matter. 1 need not urge on the Prime Minister the desirability of keeping in view the working out of some arrangement so that the representation of the maritime pi'ovinces should not be reduced. There are two ways in which this could be dealt with. It could be provided in the Quebec Bill that the population of the additional territory which ,is given to that province,' should not be taken into consideration in the computation which is made in order to ascertain the electoral unit. An amendment could be made in this Bill providing that the population in the added territory should not toe taken into the computation of the population of the provinces when you come to make up the number which has to be taken into consideration when you make a comparison between the population at one census and the population at the previous census. But, of course, legislation of that kind would not in any way remedy the difficulty which exists. If no amendment providing for the safeguards is made to these Bills we would be left to the remedy suggested by the Minister of Marine, whereby, as a result of a conference to be held between the Premiers of the provinces of the Dominion, an agreement might be made under which you would have an irreducible minimum fixed for each one of the maritime provinces, or, what would be better, a minimum fixed for all of the original provinces which entered into confederation with the addition of Prince Edward Island.
I apprehend, from the statement made by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that a conference of the provinces is to be held at which that question is to be discussed. But supposing that conference is to be held, the Premier should move, and move speedily, in order to obtain effectual results from it, by asking this 150
parliament to adopt an address to the imperial parliament, so that we would have imperial legislature in force and effect when we came to pass a redistribution Bill, and would be empowered to deal with it on that basis. The whole question of redistribution is inextricably mixed up with this problem, and it is important to have the opinion of such a conference brought to a head at an early day. My hon. friend has also told us that at some time he proposes to call the maritime provinces to council for the purpose of considering how they are to be affected by the granting of lands to the other provinces of the Dominion. When the boundaries of all the provinces are fixed as a result of these various resolutions, we shall have shut the door for ever on the possibility of any of the maritime provinces having any share in the present territory of the Dominion beyond what they have now, or on the possibility of their having any increased representation through the addition of territory, as will be the case with all the other provinces, as a result of the legislation we are now passing or may pass in the future. This problem is a very serious one. I am quite sure the Premier is sympathetic; but as a result oi this legislation, without providing in any way for our representation being unimpaired, the door is being closed against any remedy being ever obtained in that way. As far as I am concerned, I am not moving any amendment to this measure, on the faith of what I assume the Premier will do, believing that we can count on him taking such steps as are in his power to gratify the reasonable wishes of the various provinces, particularly the maritime provinces, in regard to representation. The proposition is one which ought to be taken up with regard to all the original provinces of confederation, together with Prince Edward Island. The language of section 51 with regard to this matter is well worth recalling:
On the completion of the census in the year 1871, and of each subsequent decennial census, the representation of the four provinces shall be readjusted toy such authority, in such a manner, and from such time as the parliament of Canada from time to time provides-
Subject to certain rules. Although we
have the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada and of the Privy Council based on a strictly legal interpretation of the terms of this document, it is quite evident to any hon. gentleman who has looked at the record of what occurred at the time the fathers of confederation assembled together to settle these matters, that they had in view a readjustment to be made by a comparison every ten years of the populations of the different provinces with that



of Canada consisting of the four original provinces. That that should be preserved as the basis of confederation is a proposition which is not an unreasonable one; and, realizing that though some guards could be obtained by the insertion of amendments in this Bill, but apprehending at the same time that they would be ineffectual, I ask the Premier, in connection with the various questions germane to this, which will of necessity come up in this and succeeding years, to see if he cannot work out the problem so that the representation of the various provinces will be maintained.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I realize the very great importance of the matter which the hon. gentleman has just mentioned. The maritime provinces lost a certain number of members under the census of 1901. If I remember correctly, they stand to lose five members by the census of 1911-two in New Brunswick, two in Nova Scotia, one in Prince Edward Island. The people of those provinces naturally take a deep interest in having their representation in this parliament maintained. I recall very well the debate in 1908, when those resolutions were introduced by the right hon. gentleman who now leads the opposition. The principal portion of the debate turned upon the matter which has just been mentioned by my hon. friend from Pictou. The maritime provinces, as I understand, depended on subsection 4 of section 51 as a safeguard to prevent the reduction of their representation. Subsection 4 is as follows:
On such readjustment the number of members for a province shall not be reduced unless the proportion which the number of the population of the province bore to the number of the aggregate population of Canada at the then last preceding readjustment of the number of members for the provinces is ascertained at the then latest census to be diminished by one-twentieth part or upwards.
This worked out in connection with the other portions of section 51 in this way. In the first place, you ascertained the unit of representation by dividing the population of Quebec by 65, the constant number of members to which that province is entitled. Having obtained the unit of representation in that way, it was necessary to ascertain something more before you could reduce the representation of any province. You had to ascertain whether or not the proportion which the population of the province bore to the population of all Canada, as determined at the previous census, bad been diminished by the results of that census to the extent of one-twentieth. If it had not been diminished to the extent of one-twentieth, the province would not lose any part of its representation. The difficulty which has arisen is this. Section 51 as it originally existed in the British Mr. MACDONALD.
North America Act had clearly related to the four provinces of Canada which constituted the confederation-the old provinces of Canada divided into Ontario and Quebec, the province of New Brunswick and the province of Nova Scotia. In 1904 or 1905, when this question was referred by the late administration to the Supreme Court of Canada, afterwards going on appeal to the Privy Council, it was determined by the Privy Council that the word ' Canada ' in its application to the census of 1901, meant not Canada as originally constituted, but all the provinces of Canada, including Prince Edward Island and British Columbia, which were brought into the confederation in 1871 and 1873, and also the provinces of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan, which were constituted afterwards.
At least I think the judgment of the Privy Council went that far. My hon. friend the member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley), argued the case, and he will correct me if I am not stating it accurately.
They did not state whether it included the territories or not, but it included all the provinces.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They did decide that it included Manitoba?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Therefore, the same reasoning would lead to the conclusion that it included Alberta and Saskatchewan, after they were constituted into provinces.
All the provinces.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Just one further circumstance may be mentioned in that connection, because it seems to me a very important one. I do not know on what the judgment proceeded in the Privy Council. If I remember correctly the Privy Council did not give any reasons for the judgment.
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Did they give reasons?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I had forgotten that, but at all events in the Supreme Court of Canada, some of the judges laid stress upon the contention that the British North America Act of 1871, and the British North America Act of 1886, had an important bearing upon this question, by reason of the fact that in the British North America Act of 1886 if is declared that the Act of 1867, the Act of 1871, and the Act of 1886 shall all be construed together as if they were one Act, although doubtless there are other reasons why they were constrained to come to the conclusion which I have just mentioned. Now, I would like to say in that TegaTd, that neither the Act of 1871, nor the Act of 1886, was passed for any such purpose
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And if the effect of those Acts is to prevent this safeguarding section from having the operation which it was intended to have in the first instance, then it would seem to me that there is a pretty fair argument to be made, that the compact between the provinces of Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick, which was effected by the British North America Act of 1867, has been inadvertently departed from.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), and the hon. member from St. John <,Mr. Pugs-ley), who take a great interest in this .question that all of us from the maritime provinces are just as deeply interested in it as they are, and I can assure my hon. friend from Pictou that it will have the earnest and careful consideration of the government. Various suggestions have been made as to how the representation of the maritime provinces might be maintained, but I need not go into them to-night. I will be glad to discuss them at any time with any hon. gentleman in this House, who takes an interest in this question. I think, however, it must be apparent to every one of ns who has given consideration to this question, and I have given a great deal of consideration to it, that no one of the methods suggested is free from difficulty. Doubtless some of these suggestions would be attended with less difficulty than others. One suggestion that has been made is, that a minimum representation should be established for the maritime provinces. Another suggestion is that the British North America Act should be amended, to the effect that in estimating the one-twentieth diminution which is required under the provisions of subsection 4 of section 51, only the four original provinces should be taken into consideration, so far as any diminution of the representation of those provinces is concerned. If I am right in the view that some of the judges went upon the grounds which I mentioned a moment ago, it would seem to me that perhaps that suggestion would afford the most reasonable basis for an amendment to the British North America Act.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
But I would not like to be understood as giving a final opinion in that regard1, because the importance of this question demands very much more consideration than I have been able to give it during the past four or five months, as my hon. friends in the House will understand. I can only repeat in conclusion, that my hon. friend from Pictou can rest assured 150J
that this matter will engage the very earnest and careful attention of the government.
