For the last few years boats used to call at a place called Camp Head, but I am not sure that they did last year. I am particularly anxious that that call should continue.
Yes, that call is required. That is after they pass Mackay's point.

Last year, I believe, it was obligatory upon the company to call there only while the steamer ' Marion ' was making her regular trips. It is very desirable that a steamer should call there during the whole of open navigation en route to Iona. I hope the minister will have that inserted in the contract.

I shall be very glad to look into that.
Steam service between Canada and Australia or New Zealand or both, on the Pacific Ocean, $185,509.

What was
the extent of the carrying trade last year of the line thus subsidized?

Last year twelve voyages were made.	The total
number of passengers was 6,016; freight, 53,680 tons; mail, 10,012 bags, and 937 sacks.
They are not paid extra for carrying the mail?

No, the mail carriage is provided for in the subsidy.
Steam service between Canadian Atlantic ports and Australia and New Zealand, $120,-
000.
Mr. SINCLAIR How does it come that we have two services to New Zealand?

One is on the Pacific and the other by the Atlantic ports. These vessels on the Atlantic side make a sailing once a month, on the 15th.

In the summer the service is from Montreal to Auckland, Wellington, Lyttleton and Dunedin, in New Zealand, and Melbourne and Sydney in Australia. In the winter months, they sail from St. John and Halifax and make the same terminal ports in New Zealand and Australia.
How much did they carry last year?
The total distance is nearly 13,000 miles. The freight carried was 12,304 tons by weight and 73,640 tons by measurement. There is little or no passenger traffic and no mails.
What is the tonnage of the ships in the service?
It runs from 7,503 to 9,964 tons, there being four vessels. The speed is from 10 knots to 12 knots.
Are any of these steamship subventions new, and if any are new, will the minister please indicate that as we come to them?

These are all old votes, most of the services having been established for a long series of years.
Ocean and mail service between Canada and Great Britain, $600,000.
What is the minister doing in regard to that?

The contracts end on the 1st May, 1912. The government has had under consideration, for several years, as my hon. friend knows, various plans for the improvement of the service across the Atlantic. I find records of these plans on the files as I look them over. Some of them are pretty ambitious, and all of them anticipate a large amount of money in the shape of subsidies. We are paying now for Atlantic steanieTS somewhere in the region of $700,000 or $800,000, for what we call the distinctive mail service. Many of the smaller subsidies are for freight ships, passengers constituting a very small part. The present government has had no opportunity, no time, to take up these matters and give them the consideration they merit. These projects involve two things, first a large increase in the amount of money and also contracts for a considerable period of time, because a large enterprise like this will not begin on the basis of a year-to-year arrangement. Hon. gentlemen will quite see that it has 'been impossible for us to sit down and give any real attention to the subject. After the House of Commons has ended its session and left us, we hope to be able Mr. FOSTER (N. Toronto).
to get down to that question in the course of the recess and give it real consideration. There is another proposition on foot, which is to enlarge the number of vessels at present coming into our ports as beneficiaries of the subsidy granted on a tonnage basis. I have looked into that somewhat in connection with the Post Office Department, but I have not looked into it sufficiently to make up my mind in reference to it. The committee will see from the tenor of my remarks that what is likely to take place is that the present service will be continued temporarily and that during the recess the whole matter will be taken up and the consideration given to it which it deserves.
I cannot, myself, see any better way than that. 1 do not care to make long contracts under present conditions; I would not like to make a contract under the new conditions involving, as I said, much more money and for a long term, without time for consideration. In the meantime, although we may not have all that we ought to have, we have a very creditable mail service. The style of boats, the capacity of boats, the speed of boats having constantly increased since many years ago when we commenced to talk about a fast Atlantic service. Our speed now comes up to 17 and 18 knots, and the quality, the accommodation and the outfittings of our best boats are much to be commended. But the lines which are at present running those boats are not satisfied with the development. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company is now building two very fine boats for the Pacific service, and if my information is correct, those boats will be put upon the Pacific service inside of probably twelve months. That will relieve the present boats on the Pacific line for service elsewhere. There are also being built by steamship companies, improved boats, some of which will carry upon the Atlantic line. Last year, I think it was, the ' Laurentic ' and the ' Megantic ' of the Dominion-White Star line came to the river St. Lawrence and the port of Montreal. I think these vessels will also come this season, and it is not impossible that one or two other vessels of that line may make voyages to our ports.
There is one thing in connection with the St. Lawrence route which is not satisfactory, and that is that we have not so far been able to take out from Montreal the amount of freight that is offered at Montreal, and that might go via Montreal provided we had the tonnage. We have some 22 regular vessels coming into port there, large vessels, but they carry large numbers of passengers and large quantities of parcel freight, and they take a minimum of grain, according as their space is filled or is not filled. These boats, both

passenger and mail boats, are not able to take away the grain that offers at the port of Montreal, and last year, as in previous years, and as will occur no doubt next year, to a certain extent, grain will seek its way out through the port of Montreal and will not find in that class of ship tonnage sufficient to carry it. The difficulty is, coming down to the point, that the insurance rates are so high that any other than a regular steamer does not find it convenient or profitable, and maybe does not find it possible, to compete for grain from the port of Montreal. If you take the zone below us to the Atlantic ports of the United States, and compare the insurance rates with ours, our insurance rates are very much higher, and the difference in rates is sufficient to keep the tramp steamers from visiting the Montreal ports. There ought, to be some method of solution by which lower insurance charges should be given to the irregular vessels coming into our more northern harbours. We have spent an immense amount of money on the St. Lawrence route and on the gulf, in lighting, and in all the conveniences for the warning of ships. We have a route there that we might well be proud of, which has been the interest of all governments since Canada had a government, and which can claim from both parties and all governments, and has received, fair and generous consideration. There has been a progressive diminution of casualties, consequent upon the increase of lights and appliances for warning vessels. Now it does seem as though the great insurance companies, and Lloyds is of course the greatest, ought to have some regard to that progressive feature in our marine history, and ought to come a little nearer to accommodating itself in the way of insurance rates to the wants and necessities of the St. Lawrence route and the Canadian ports.
Does the minister know how much higher they are now?
I have not the figures by me, but they are considerably higher.
They have been very materially reduced in the last five years.

They have been reduced if you take a period of some length of time; but in the last two or three years, if my memory serves me right, the reductions have not been large. I may say that that matter is not escaping the attention of the government, my own department is taking that matter up, and I hope that in some way or other we may turn over a new leaf with reference to that matter, and that we may get for our ports and our trade a better insurance rate, which would enable us to remove from
ourselves the reproach of allowing the grain that offers itself to our ports to go to other .ports, owing to our lack of tonnage accommodation.
What is the speed of the new Canadian Pacific Railway boats that are going on the Atlantic?
The new boats will have a speed of not less than 22 knots.
We are to understand that, pending a review of the whole subject and a final arrangement, the contracts as they stand now will run during this year?
I am not saying that certainly, but that is the conclusion towards which the remarks I have made trend. Something might happen that would make it different, but I do not know of anything at present.
I was going to suggest to my hon. friend that he let one of these items stand over, as there are some gentlemen who are not here who would like to speak upon them.
We will leave the last item over, with the understanding that they may all be discussed.

My hon. friend mentioned the grain business. My judgment is that one of the most immediate needs of solving the difficulty about the grain business is to have more elevator accommodation at the St. Lawrence and Atlantic ports. We have not one-tenth part of the storage accommodation for grain which is needed east of the lakes. At Buffalo they have storage capacity for fifty million bushels of grain, and the result is that Buffalo has become a favourite place for the storage of grain, and when it is stored there at the proper time, and the market is satisfactory and freights are satisfactory, and tonnage is available, grain goes forward from that port to the markets of the old world. Our elevator accommodation east of the lakes is very limited in character. I am satisfied that the railway companies feel it. I have talked with the officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and they know that they Tealize that the elevator accommodation is not what it ought to be, but, of course, the railway companies usually move along under the pressure of business. It seems to me that the government ought to consider whether, at, certain important points, a large amount of storage for grain should not be provided. I am satisfied that it would go a long way towards relieving the difficulty caused by congestion, and that the grain would go forward as tonnage was available and as the market suited

I am glad to see that the minister is taking an interest in the question of insurance in the river and gulf of St. Lawrence. There is a certain amount of prejudice among the underwriters in England against the St. Lawrence route. They, of course, make their calculations, upon the losses that they make from year to year during a given period of years and they will give you that as a reason why the rates are so much higher. I am certain that the situation is not well understood by the brokers in London. They close down very early in the season on insurance in the St. Lawrence; I think it is in October
They raise their rates.

Yes, they raise their rates in October just at the time when the grain is being moved and at a time when the season is the busiest. There is no real reason in the condition of our climate why the rates should be raised so early in the season, because October and November are just as safe for navigation in the St. Lawrence as any other month. They raise their rates from Quebec away down to the Baie de Chaleur, Miramichi bay and northern coast of New Brunswick which affects the timber trade to some extent. It is quite true that tramp vessels do not find their way very much to the St. Lawrence largely on that account. Not only is the insurance all the year around too high, but it is very much heavier at the time of the year when the large bulk of the work is being done. I do not know whether anything can be done, but I think it would be a very good thing if the minister should get in touch with Lloyds people in London and give them the charts of the St. Lawrence and all the information that is available in the department in order to show them that navigation in these waters is quite safe in these early months of winter. If he does perhaps some of this prejudice, which I feel certain exists there, can be removed.

I would like to intimate to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that some time before the close of the session I wish to discuss the matter of a fast Atlantic steamship service. I will not do it to-night but I will give him notice at some later date.

I would like to ask the minister with respect 10 the service between Moncton and Bay of Fundy ports. I cannot see that provision has been made for it this year. It was for a steamer plying between Moncton and ports in the county of Cumberland, Nova Scotia, and in the county of Albert, New Brunswick. I think the amount paid last year was $2,000.

I think my hon. friend will find an item before^ we get through in reference to that. I just want to say in connection with the point mentioned by the hon. member for Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair), that we have been making representations in two ways. We have been making representations by way of spreading information as to what has been done in improving, lighting and other conveniences in Canada and we have also been making representations, and we are at the present time making representations, to the insurance companies themselves and endeavouring not only to put all the information which we possess before them but to put it before them in such a way that we are getting them to canvass it and to talk over it with us. If anything can be done in that way during the present year to make everything as plain as it can be made, I propose that my department shall have that done. I do not think there will be any lack in that respect. In reference to the suggestion of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) that the solution of this matter would be the building of elevators, I do not want it to be understood here that the government propose to take over the duty and the work that belongs to the railway companies whose business it is to equip their roads with these terminal conveniences. Wherever the government has railways and termini and grain offers and those conveniences are necessary, I think the government will not be backward in providing them. As far as the great railway companies are concerned, I think they must themselves provide terminal conveniences. It is their duty to do it and I see no reason Why we should not impress that duty upon them.

In connection with this question of grain elevators, I think that the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) perhaps does not bear in mind the fact that a very large proportion of the wheat that comes from the northwest is distributed in Ontario and the other provinces. The object of the elevator companies is not simply to make what they can in the way of charges for holding the grain over for the winter but it is the money made in the elevating of the grain and, in turn, discharging it into cars that is important to them. We have several places in Ontario to-day where large milling companies have erected grain elevators. There is a great deal of the spirit of gambling in connection with grain and while to-day the miller aims at buying grain when it is low, in order to accommodate the grain that he owns himself, he must have an elevator of his own. I have in mind two or three flour-milling companies in Ontario who have large elevator accommodation. I think it is hardly fair to expect the rail-

way companies, as a business enterprise, to build huge elevators, have them filled up with grain in the fall of the year and simply derive the charge from handling or storing it during the winter. This is a matter that, in my judgment, in so far as Ontario is concerned, will correct itself inasmuch as the flour milling companies will construct and maintain elevators of their own and thus relieve the congestion of grain at the eastern lake ports.
Steam service between Canada and Cuba, $25,000.
What business did this line do last year?
The Canada and Cuba line did not do much of a business, and as far as I am concerned it will not go on the same another year.
It is from St. John, is it not?

Well, it was. They made nine passages, they carried no passengers, they carried out 35,325 tons by measurement, and they brought back not a single ounce of cargo. When the service was first projected, it was with the idea that these steamers should carry things to Cuba, and carry things back from Cuba to Canada. What it has resulted in is that they carry out a certain large amount of produce from Canada, but after reaching Cuba they load up for foreign ports. Hereafter the service may touch at Cuba and do good work in carrying produce out of Cuba, but it has got to be so connected as to bring back something for Canada or else they will not get a subsidy.

That matter is worthy of further consideration by the minister. The important thing for Canada is to get a foreign market for Canadian products, and why should we 'be so anxious to buy goods in Cuba and spend Canadian money there? The minister tells us that the line to Australia and New Zealand has carried out forty thousand odd tons; does that mean the same measurement as he gave for the Cuba line?
That means tons weight.

Let us suppose that at least half the quantity of Canadian products is sent to Cuba for this small subsidy of $25,000 as is sent to Australia and New Zealand for the large subsidy of $180,000, and the showing is not so bad after all. This subsidy was given for the purpose of developing the trade in potatoes, particularly between the maritime province ports and Cuba and it has been very effective in that respect. As to passengers, of course it is natural to expect
that passengers would go to New York and take a passenger steamer there rather than travel by a freight boat. It has been explained to me by those in the enterprise that really there is not much return cargo from Cuba to Canada.
I think that is so.

We continued the subsidy as an encouragement for the export of Canadian products, and to give our people a foreign market, and in doing that we were accomplishing the most important object to be gained by this small subsidy. I have no doubt that the Minister of Trade and Commerce will look into the matter carefully before he takes any action.

The position taken by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley), is very interesting when we contrast it with the position he took last year in regard to this matter. When these subsidies were up last year I called attention to the fact that so far as the trade between Canada and Australia and New Zealand was concerned the outgoing trade from Canada consisted almost entirely of manufactured articles, principally agricultural implements, and that the export of Canadian agricultural products to these countries was a mere bagatelle. The incoming trade from Australia and New Zealand to Canada consisted mainly of agricultural products which were coming in here and competing with the products of our own farmers. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley), now says that we should look mainly at these subsidies from the standpoint of getting outside markets, for our products, but last year.he was willing to subsidize steamship lines to convey our manufactured articles to Australia and New Zealand, and to bring back to Canada agricultural products to compete with the products raised by our own farmers.
That was-getting a foreign market for our manufactures.

Yes, but the hon. gentleman and his political friends represented themselves as the friends of the agriculturists, when in that respect they were showing themselves the friends of the .manufacturers, and the foes of the agriculturists, because they were subsidizing steamship lines to bring back agricultural products which they proposed to let into the country free, to compete with our own agricultural products, while the outgoing agricultural exports from Canada did not amount to a bagatelle. It seems to me that this whole matter of steamship subsidies could be very well looked1 into with a great deal of care. I have never been able to understand on what basis these subsidies have been granted;

whether the steamers were supposed to be paid so much a trip or whether the subsidy was paid on the amount of tonnage carried inwards and outwards. It does seem to me that the volume of trade with some of these countries to which we subsidize steamship lines does not warrant the amount of the subsidy granted. The Auditor General's report for the year ending 31st March, 1911, shows that a subsidy was granted between Canada and Mexico of $125,000 which I suppose includes the service on the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, and of that amount $11,458.34 was not used. Then, $50,000 was granted for the Canada-New Zealand1 service, and none of it was used. Between the Canadian Atlantic ports and Australia and New Zealand there was a subsidy of $120,000 granted which I believe is to be voted again this year, and $20,000 of that was not used. I notice that in several of these items here the full amount voted was not used. That is why I ask on what basis these grants are voted. I would also like some, explanation as to why they have not all been used'.

The grants have not all been used because the money has not all been earned according to contract. There is a gross sum put in the estimates, which forms the maximum of the contract for a certain number of trips. The vessels are paid generously so much per trip. If they do not make the full number of trips, they do not get the full amount of the subsidy. A contract is entered into for each of these services. There are certain general features common to all the contracts; then there are special features which fit the individual case.
In arriving at the amount you are going to pay, do you take into account the value of the goods they carry out of Canada and the value of the goods they bring back ?

I do not think that is taken as a basis. There arp some services which are called services of necessity; there are others which are experimental. You do not get as much trade as you would like to get. You are working up a trade. If there were a full trade, there would be no necessity for the subsidy at all. The arrangement is for each individual service, and there is the usual bargaining between the steamship company and the government. If a lump sum is arranged for a certain number of voyages, for each complete round trip, the company gets_ its proportion of the whole subsidy. If it does not make the number of trips stipulated for, as a maximum, the payment falls short in that proportion. It would be almost impossible, in such ser-Mr. EDWARDS.
vices, to pay according to the amount of exports and imports, from the fact that you start a service, not because there is a plethora of freight offering to and fro, but because you want to work up to a larger and larger commercial intercourse. You will help the vessel at the first, and in course of time, some of these become paying and do not need subsidies.
I would assume that in asking for a subsidy they would advance some argument to show why a subsidy should be granted.
There is no doubt they advance arguments.

It seems to me they ought to have something more tangible in the way of an argument than simply that they want the money. I would suppose that they would present arguments to show that such a trade could be worked up.

I do not think my hon. friend is ingenious enough to invent any argument that has not already been used by the companies as a reason why they should get a subsidy. But I will teli my hon. friend what I am doing. He will find in a report which is now in the printer's hands, and will soon be in the hands of the House, a statement with reference to every one of these subsidies. The salient terms of the contract are given, the capacity of the vessel, its speed, tonnage, etc. Then, there is the gross amount of what it carries in passengers, mails and freight. Next year this report will contain not only the gross amount of freight carried each way, but an analysis of the principal grades carried, so that there will be an opportunity t of judging not only whether or not we are carrying a certain amount of dead weight, but what is the quality of the merchandise that is going and coming-whether it is all timber all agricultural produce, all manufactured goods, or, if not, what proportion and quantity of each. I have also come to the conclusion to insert in all the contracts that are made this year a clause asking the company to present a full account of its expenses and of its receipts, so that we shall be able to find out just about what is the outgo and the income; and when we arrive at a certain point, we shall be able to say to the company: Your passenger traffic has increased and your freight traffic has increased, your expenses have been so much, and your receipts have been so much, you have been able to pay a certain dividend, or you have not. In that way I think we shall get down to a better basis upon which we can adjust the subsidy to each case in hand. There will alwavs be cases where there will be a necessity for communication hut where

there is no possibility, within a short period at least, of a paying trade.
Will that statement be a solemn declaration or one made on oath?

I think we may assume that we shall get at the rights of the case. If we find that the accounts are not given properly, we will take measures to get them, because that is a condition of these companies getting subsidies. But I prefer to go on the assumption that the steamship companies with which we make these contracts will give us a fair statement of their returns.
Steam service or services between Canada and Newfoundland, $18,000.

Before Christmas I mentioned to the hon. minister a proposal which had been made for a daily service. I understand that the new boat for this line has come out, and that the trade between Canada and Newfoundland is rapidly increasing. I hope the minister has given favourable consideration to the proposition to assist in extending this service so as to secure a daily service between North Sydney and Port aux Basques.
How frequent is it now?

Three times a week. A short time ago I was informed that the freight at North Sydney accumulates to such an extent that the Intercolonial Railway has been compelled to refuse freight for shipment at certain seasons of the year because of the impossibility of moving it fast enough by the present tri-weekly service.
Mr. FOSTER (North Toronto) There is a continual growth in the trade. Last year there were carried 6,765 first-class passengers, 11,178 second-class passengers, 15,538 tons of freight, and 1,635 head of stock, with a very large quantity of mail, and if you take that trade in conjunction with the previous three years there is a gratifying increase. The company had the misfortune to lose their vessel. They have their new boat out now, I think, but I am not sure if she is on the service. However, the supplementary estimates are yet to come down, and before that takes place the matter will be considered. I may say that so far as I am concerned, I am very sympathetic with that trade and that route, and I think we ought not to be over parsimonious in forwarding the interests of that line of communication all that we possibly can.
Hear, hear.

I am very glad indeed that the hon. member for Pictou has directed the attention of the minister to this service. I am particularly concerned
in the matter because this service haS its terminus on the Canadian side in my own town. I am pleased to be able to tell the minister that the ' New Bruce,' as she is called, left the other side a few weeks ago and has made her trip direct into the port of North Sydney. There are several pleasing features about this service. We are glad to get a very excellent boat on this route. It is now making regular trips backward and forward between Port aux Basques and North Sydney. Another thing that has been proven is, that this boat has been able at the hardest period of the winter, about the last of February, to make her way through the ice from Newfoundland to North Sydney. Thus we have the certainty of another outlet from Canada to Newfoundland, and from Newfoundland across to this side. In this connection I would like to ask the minister how much was paid for this service last year.
Last year about $9,000.
I notice that the minister has $18,000 in the estimates this year. Is it the intention to give that amount to the company provided they put on another boat ?

The $18,000 is available for a daily service. The present tri-weekly service, if I am not mistaken, is to be made a daily service. In Newfoundland there is to be a daily service by train, so that a very great improvement is looked for both by Newfoundland and by ourselves in the communications this year.
Steam service between Canada and South Africa, $146,000.

I may say with reference to this item, that the development of trade between Canada and South Africa has been very satisfactory. For a long service it probably has been the most satisfactory we have had, and the trade shows signs of constant improvement.
Where do the vessels sail from ?

The contract requires sailings from Montreal, calling at Quebec and at any other Canadian ports during the summer, and from St. John and Halifax in the winter. Last year there were twelve voyages. The number of passengers carried is not many by that route. There were carried 26 passengers, 31,385 tons of freight and 37,800 tons in measurement. There were carried besides, a considerable quantity of live stock, and I will say for the Elder-Dempster people that they show a very commendable ac-

tivity in. canvassing freight throughout Canada for that service. They issue a weekly letter, and send their men out, and they are actively at work getting freight.
What is the character of the goods carried?

That I cannot tell exactly, except from having simply seen some oi the invoices. However, the character of the goods is very varied. Quite a large quantity of flour is taken, also implements and largely general manufactures. In another year I hope to have a thorough tabulation of these goods.
Have you only one commercial agent in South Africa?
We have only one agent there.
At Durban?
Yes, he is at Durban. It appears from the statistics that Durban is by far the largest port.
The finest too.

It is by far the largest port, and it strikes more at the centre of the country as well.
Steam service between Halifax and Newfoundland via Cape Breton ports, $4,000.
At what ports in Cape Breton did this boat call last year?

A lot of ports. The vessel starts from Halifax and goes to the west coast o.f Newfoundland. It calls at St. Peters, Grand Narrows, Baddeck, North Sydney, South Sydney, Ingonish, Neil's Harbour, and Aspey bay in Cape Breton; and also St. Paul's Island, Bay St. George, Codroy, Bay of Islands and Bonne bay.
The vessel makes a round trip calling at the same ports each way?
The same ports each way.

How frequent is the service?
Mr. FOSTER (North Toronto.) The vessel made fifteen round trips last year, and carried 180 passengers, 8,558 tons of freight, and some mail.
The passenger list may not be very large, hut I may say in support of the service that it is a very useful one in the interests of the fishermen at these different ports of call.

I understood the member for Pictou to say that the only ser-Mr. FOSTER (N. Toronto).
vice between Cape Breton and Newfoundland was a tri-weekly one. It seems to me that there are other services which would appear to be independent of the one to which he refers.

The service from Canada to Newfoundland runs between the Dominion and the colony from the nearest possible points. It is a passenger line of communication. The service between Halifax and Newfoundland, via Cape Breton ports, starts from Halifax and runs through, I think, the Bras d'Or lakes and round the coast of Cape Breton.
Through the Bras d'Or lakes.
The service goes to some of the outports of Newfoundland.
On the west coast.

The service covering Halifax, St. John's, Newfoundland and Liverpool, I think, is a service run in conjunction with the Newfoundland government, and affords communication between the other side and Newfoundland.
Steam service between Halifax, St. John's, Newfoundland, and Liverpool, $20,000,

I am informed that that is simply a freight service carrying no passengers, but chiefly deals, competing in this trade with the tramp _ ships. I never could understand why a line should be subsidized to carry deals to the west coast of England, for that is a commodity that is in the market all the time and should be left to open competition. That subsidy has been on the list for many years, and I have never been able to get a satisfactory explanation of it.

I do not know that I can give my hon. friend much more information than he has. The contract is with the Furness-Withy Company. The subsidy is an old stager-I remember it away back. I see one good thing about it-they have to carry trade commissioners over and back free. Last year they made twenty-five round trips; not many passengers-16 in, 48 out, total 64; freight 114,357 tons weight.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is it shown how much of that is deals?

No; I
was explaining before my hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) came in that we will have a tabulation of the different kinds of freight so that we may know what business is doing.
They made a lot of money carrying apples.

They have been charging very high rates, I understand. I think the minister should look into that and see i! he could not reduce the rates on apples from Nova Scotia to England. I am told that the rates ruling last autumn were something like 90 cents from the Annapolis valley to Liverpool or London. That is a very lucrative business for a ship. I know very many ship owners who would like to have the carrying of these apples at 50 cents a barrel. A small part of the rate charged, I understand, goes to the railway. There may have been changes in that rate on account of the Canadian Pacific railway coming in. If we are going to subsidize a vessel to carry apples, I think we should have some control over the rates.

I suppose the apple growers would like to have the rates as low as possible, but what they are more troubled about is that the apples do not get there in a sufficiently short space of time-the rate of going is not quick enough to take the apples to market in the best condition. A delegation of the apple growers came to see me, and we had a talk over the matter. I am going to try, if possible, to get a little quicker transit.
How long do they take to go across?
They run at 11 knots-perhaps not quite that. I think the growers want to get the apples there in about six days.
Do not these contracts provide that the government shall have control over the rates?

Yes, most of these large contracts. But there are difficulties in that which have always been faced, but never met. It is a orettv difficult thing for the minister sitting in his office to say what the freight rates should be. The freight rates go up and they go down. I think it would be an advantage to have some board or authority on freight rates to assist the minister to come to a conclusion as to what are really equitable rates. In some of the contracts it is provided that they shall not charge more than is charged by vessels from New York to the ports to which they trade. That forms a basis of comparison that is apparent. But when a complaint comes to the minister that they are charging too much on apples or on cheese, the knowledge or the arts of the steamship company generally get away with the minister, and he feels that he is not quite big enough to pass judgment on the point. There has been a large increase in freight rates recently. Charters have gone up and vessels are in great demand. All freight carrying steamers have increased1 their rates.
We have had protests against that from shippers. But when you go to the steamship companies showing an increase m rates all over, it makes it difficult to say that there shall not be an increase in rates even by a subsidized steamer. The argument on the other side is that a subsidy is given for the purpose of making the rates a little lower than would be the case by an unsubsidized vessel and there is a good deal in that argument. But in order to find a solution of the difficulty I hope to get some authoritative adviser who will make it his business to look after these things, and who, will be able to advise the department as to what is right, and I hope to have that in the course of the next year.

The minister has stated that this is a very old service and I am sure it would be the desire of the minister to make this service as useful as possible. Conditions in eastern Nova Scotia have changed a good deal since the commencement of this service. The minister knows that now, in eastern Nova Scotia, we have a large population who have come over from the other side of the water within the last nine or ten years. There is a large passenger traffic now to and from the old country and eastern Nova Scotia which was entirely unknown fifteen or twenty years ago. There would also be some freight traffic such as the exportation of canned lobsters dried fish and that sort of thing, which would go direct to the old country if there was opportunity. I think the minister could easily make this boat call at the terminus of the Intercolonial at North Sydney, or some other point on Sydney harbour, and give the large number of people at that place who go across to the old country and return, and people who may wish to come directly to the steel and coal works at North Sydney, an opportunity of reaching that point directly by this service. At present these people have to come up via Montreal, and sometimes from New York, at a much larger expense and more inconvenience. I hope the minister will give this matter some consideration.

I will look into it.
Steam service from the opening to the closing of navigation in 1912 between the mainland and the Magdalen Islands, $15,000.
The contract ends in 1913. The service starts from the town of Pictou.

I received a letter from the Halifax Board of Trade which unfortunately I have not before me. I have no doubt that the minister has seen a copy of the letter. It urges that this service should start from the port of Hali-

fax. It seems to me that Halifax would be the proper port from which to make this service start. A great deal of the business done with the Magdalen Islands originates at the port of Halifax, and it merely means starting from Halifax and calling at Pictou.

The matter has already been taken into consideration so far as the contract having been awarded is now running and I do not propose to break the contract. If my hon. friend will take the map and will look at the Magdalen Islands, he will conclude that there is no better point than Pictou from which to start this communication. It is on the line of the Intercolonial railway, and it is the nearest possible point to the Magdalen Islands from anything like a large port.

If the frequency of the service demands a shorter distance between the point of departure and the Magdalen Islands, there would be some force in the statement of the minister. But what is the service?

It does not run in the winter time. But in the summer season it made 61 trips, carrying 1,416 passengers, 6,173 tons of freight and 1,269 head of live stock, hops, sheep, cattle, etc., and mail bags galore. So far as I know, it is a well conducted service.

I have no doubt about that. But I say that inasmuch as the service is but twice a week, there seems to be no reason why the steamer should not start from the port of Halifax^ because that is the port that does the business with the Magdalen Islands. I do not understand the Halifax Board of Trade to urge that the steamer should not call at Pictou; I can quite understand that that would create some prejudice in that old historic port. But I say that this service might well start from Halifax and serve the Magdalen Islands two trips per week. It would riot hurt, in.the slightest degree, the port of Pictou or any other port. Of course, it might be _ that the steamer would require some additional subsidy.
' Mr. FOSTER (North Toronto). I was wondering while my hon. friend was speaking, what would have happened to-night in the last five minutes if the fortunes of war had kept my hon. friend at Lunenburg instead of sending him to Halifax.

I am looking after the interests of my constituents.
Mr. HUGHES (Kings, P. E. I.) It would be simply impossible for this boat to make two trips a week between Halifax and the Magdalen Islands. The whole six days of the week are taken up now in mak-Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).
ing the two trips from Pictou. The steamer has to call at several places on the way to the Magdalen Islands, and I think it takes her five days and a half to make the two trips. The suggestion of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) is simply impossible.
I am afraid my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has not been properly briefed. His information on the subject is very scanty and entirely inaccurate.
He is new to his constituency as yet.

My hon. friend from Kings, Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hughes) has very effectually disposed of the suggestion he has made. I could summon as a witness my hon. friend the ex-Postmaster General, who represented the Magdalen Islands for a number of years, and who can testify as to the excellent service and the splendid character of the boat, and the fact that under the existing contract a better service is being rendered than has been rendered for the last 40 years. There has never been any suggestion from the Magdalen Islands that this service should start from Halifax. Whether it is that because the constituency is represented by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) and by my very able friend here (Mr. MacleanV Halifax has got so ambitious that it wants to get all the steamship subsidies, I do not know, but there does not appear to be any other possible reason why they should have asked for this.

The desire of the inhabitants of the islands is that the service should be between Pictou, Prince Edward Island and the Magdalen Islands twice a week, but probably the islanders would like to have the service with Halifax because there are several months in the year when the service is closed. The service between Pictou and the Magdalen Islands is in operation only during the summer months, the fall and the spring. But, it is quite possible, during the winter, to send one or two government steamers or ice-breakers, from Halifax.
Or Sydney.
From Halifax or Sydney to the Magdalen Islands.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We did that this year.
Mr. LKM1KUA. Yes. 1 congratulate my hon. friend upon having done that.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: A most successful voyage.
I congratulate my hon. friend upon that. I tried during several years to have that done, but we were always told by the captains that they could not reach,the islands in the winter time.
There is a different government in power.
By what steamer was the service performed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My recollection is that the ' Stanley ' made one trip and that it was a most successful trip. We are going to have another voyage before the season closes.

In that case I would ask the hon. gentleman to suppress that political marconigram which is sent every week now that, through the good offices of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, communication has been established.
Now that you have the marconigram you might take away the other service.
No, I prefer the service.

I would like to give the minister notice that before the next estimates are prepared I shall be better informed as to the claims of the port of Halifax and if provision is not asked for in connection with this service I shall ask for a new one altogether.
Steam service between Makone bay and Taneook island, $1,000.

I would like to call the attention of the minister to a petition that I forwarded to him a few days ago asking for a small subsidy for a steamship service between the ports of Arichat and Canso. These ports were served some years ago by one steamship company. The service was from Canso to Arichat and Port Mulgrave. But a few years ago the service was separated and one boat was put on between Canso and Mulgrave and another between Arichat and Mulgrave. In that way the service between these two important ports became disconnected. I would be very glad if the minister would give his attention to this matter before preparing the supplementary estimates and I would hope that he would see his way clear to putting $1,000 in the estimates this year for this service. Another request has been forwarded to the department in connection with the steamship service between Halifax, Petit de Grat, d'Escouse: and River Bourgeois, all ports on the island of Cape Breton. These are important places, they have no communication by railway, they have no means of shipping the products of their industry to Halifax or elsewhere. I would urge that the minister would be good enough to also give attention to that request and endeavour, if possible, to provide a small subsidy of $2,000 for this service during the coming year.
I will be very glad to give these matters attention.

I have been asked by the people of Canso to press that matter upon the minister's attention and I would like him to give his best consideration to this proposed service between Arichat and Canso.
Steamship service from the opening to the closing of navigation in 1912, between Port Mulgrave, St. Peter's, Irish Cove and Marble Mountain and other ports on the Bras d'Or lakes, $6,000.

The steamship performing this service is giving a good service to that part of the country. I think this service should be confined entirely to ports in the Bras d'Or lakes. It is a sea run of about seventy miles from the canal to the head of navigation in East bay, and the boat will have all she can do without going to Mulgrave at all. I submit to the minister that it is not desirable to be giving subsidies to steamships where they are in competition with railways. There is a railway from the canal at St. Peter's connecting with the Intercolonial railway at Point Tupper and any passengers or freight or anything else that the steamer ' Richmond ' would bring to St. Peter's could be put on the railway there and carried to their destination. This boat is running from the canal to Mulgrave in competition with the Intercolonial railway and Cape Breton railway from Point Tupper to St. Peter's and in that way giving a service to a section of country which, I am sure, does not really require it, whereas such ports as Big Pond, the head of East bay and several other places in the Bras d'Or lakes, are in need of this service. Passengers and goods could be carried from these ports to meet the railway at the Grand Narrows. The boat should be kept here altogether without going up to Alulgrave, where there is no real necessity for it. I wish to direct the attention of the minister to this matter because I want him to apply the subsidy where he will get the best work done and where he will not be in competition with railways.
Mr. FOSTER (North Toronto.) There is a large family of children here., that I find under my care. Some of them cropped up a good while ago and I know their faces, while there are others that are entirely new to me. This one deserves some consideration. This boat made 204 round trips and she carried on an average nine passengers per trip and two and a quarter tons of freight. The $6,000 subsidy, if we calculated it on the basis of the freight that was carried, would put us in the

position of paying $12 for every ton of freight that was moved. She has either to go somewhere else and get some more freight or else we are paying, seemingly, a very large amount for a service that does not appear to have very much in it. If it were growing it would not be so bad, but it does not seem to be growing. I think there is something' in what my hon. friend says that we are trying to run against a couple of railways and we are getting the bad end of it.

The service of the steamer ' Richmond * outside of the Bras d'Or lake is for the accommodation largely of the important communities of Marble mountain and West bay in the Bras d'Or lake, and d'Escouse, Poulamond and Lennox in the Lennox passage.
At Marble Mountain the Dominion Coal Company have extensive works, and from that point they ship dolamite which is used in the manufacture of iron and steel. The railway between Point Tupper and St. Peter's is unfortunately owned by a private corporation. Now, a car of flour, ordered by a merchant at Marble Mountain, passes over the Intercolonial to Mulgrave, is. shipped on the Cape Breton railway to St. Peter's and from St. Peter's it has to be transported by steamer to Marble Mountain. That would mean that three rates would have to be paid by the merchant at Marble Mountain on a carload of flour from Ontario. The service has been maintained two days a week from Bras D'Or lake to Port Mulgrave for the purpose of taking passengers from these points not touched by a railway and also for carrying freight which is shipped by the Intercolonial railway to Mulgrave. This service enables the people there to get a very much cheaper rate than if they were obliged to pay the Intercolonial railway, the Cape Breton railway, and then the freight rate on the boat.

I corroborate what has been said by my hon. friend (Mr. Kyte) with regard to this service. Marble Mountain is sixteen miles from the railway, and this is actually the only service the people there have. If this boat does not connect with Port Mulgrave, the people of Marble Mountain will not be able to get to the railway unless they drive rifteen or sixteen miles over a mountain. West Bay is in the same position except that it is closer to the Intercolonial railway than Marble Mountain. I would be very sorry, indeed, if the service were changed because these people living there would be set back to the condition they were in fifty years ago.

I did not say I was going to change the service this year, but I said it would bear looking into. I think that in some of these services there Mr. FOSTER (N. Toronto).
is a duplication and in some cases a triplication, and while I do no<t propose to disturb them very much this year, it is worth keeping tab bn them to see whether a redisposition could not be made which would give a better service and perhaps not cost us as much.

If the Cape Breton Railway Company which runs thirty miles of a road from Point Tupper to St. Peter were worth its salt, it would run its line down to the waters of the Bras D'Or lake on the canal, which is only about a quarter of a mile from the end of its line now. Then the traffic from North Mountain and all these points would simply be run down to the end of the line, and thus all this duplication would be done away with. As the railway is located now it is a little piece from the water, and the freight has to be carried from the head of the canal to the terminus of this railway. It shows a tremendous lack of enterprise on the part of that company that they do not connect with the Bras D'Or lakes, and put themselves into a condition to receive the freight. Then an arrangement could be made with the Intercolonial railway and the freight would run right into the ports on the Bras D'Or lakes, and thus avoid the difficulty we now have to contend with.

I would remind the minister that the difficulty which my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) seems to have with respect to the connection there, will be altogether avoided the moment the present government carries out the policy of acquiring the branch line railways. Then, I will be willing that the service outside the Bras D'Or lakes shall be discontinued.
Steam service from the opening to the closing of navigation in 1912, between Pictou and Chetieamp, $2,000.
Could the minister give us some information with regard to this service?
This steamship line carried 227 passengers, making twenty-six and a half round trips; 1,173 tons of freight by weight, and 310 tons by measurement.	.

Is it the intention that this boat will call at the ports of Arisaig, Georgeville, Ballantyne's Cove and Morristown, during the coming season. These ports intervene between Pictou and Chetieamp, and I understand that the steamer ' Electra ' which gave the service, only called occasionally at those ports, or whenever it suited the captain. The people along that shore had a grievance inasmuch as the service was very irregular and when they remonstrated they were told that the boat was receiving no

subsidy for calling at points in Antigonish
county and therefore they could not expect any improvement in that respect. Last year, an arrangement was made that the boat should call at these points and be paid an extra subsidy. In some way or other which is not necessary to explain just now the amount was not provided for in the estimates, and the arrangement was made with the captain that if he undertook to perform the service, as soon as the money could be obtained he would be paid. A service was then given which was fairly satisfactory. I had communication with the minister on the matter last year. I wish to ask the present Minister of Trade and Commerce if it is the intention to carry on that service next year. The points on the route that I have mentioned are distant from the railway on an average of twenty miles. Arisaig is about eighteen miles from the Intercolonial railway, Ballantyne's Cove twenty-five miles, and Morristown seventeen miles from the Intercolonial railway. In the spring and fall, when the roads are in bad condition, the people get their supplies in from Pictou by this steamer, and the service is the only convenience they have in that respect. I hope the minister will look into that matter.
The service _ will be continued between the two terminal points, and all the accommodation that can be given will be given. I have not been able to go into the matter thoroughly yet.
I wish to know whether the extra subsidy was paid last year.
It was not paid; there was no contract.
Was there not an offer on the part of the department that if the service were performed it would be paid for?

If the department although I was not the minister, made a bona fide offer that they would be paid in so far as they carried out the service, they will be paid. I do not intend to go back on the arrangement if I find that it was bona fide made by the minister.
Is it the intention of the department to continue the service this year as usual between Mul-grave and Cheticamp P

I am not prepared to say that it will be continued just as usual. The service will be continued, but this is one of the cases in which I am looking to see whether it is not pos-1
sible to avoid a triplication of services, and get just as good or perhaps a better service. Anyway, it will not be any worse.

This is a very important item to my constituency, particularly to the north end of the county, where we have not any railways as yet, though we hope to have one in a short time. If a change is going to be made in the line, as I am told is the intention, I am afraid the service will not be improved. I think it is the intention to have one boat do the service from Pictou to Mulgrave and from Mulgrave to Cheticamp, calling at certain ports on the way, and going back to Mulgrave, making the trip twice a week. This to my mind is impossible, if we are to have a satisfactory service.	I hope the minister will look
into this matter carefully. If he makes a contract with some company that pretends to be able to do this, and is not able, it will be a serious thing for our people, who depend on this service as their only means of communication. I admit that there has been some duplication of the service, but I confess that I do not know of any other solution than the continuation of the service as it is. If a better or even as good a service can be had, I shall be satisfied, but I would be sorry if our people suffered from not having as good a service.

We will try to avoid that.
Steam service between Prince Edward Island and Cape Breton and Newfoundland, $12,000.

Last summer or the summer before last, an application was made by the-people of North Inverness to have this boat call at Cheticamp in order to help along the cattle trade. The government or the company sent down an officer to determine whether there was water enough in the eastern harbour to permit the boat to call, and I think the report was that there was a scarcity of water. I understand that some dredging is to be done there quite early in the coming summer, so that it will then be possible for this boat to call. I think the company were willing that the boat should call if there was enough water.
Steam service between Quebeo and Gaspd Basin, touching at intermediate ports, $8,500.

I would like to relieve the anxiety of the contractors for this service, who are Quebec gentlemen, Bouchard brothers. They have spent a considerable amount in getting the proper vessel to ply between these various ports, and they have been very good to the public. When I was the member for the county, they used to send me 25 or 30 passes for poor people.

Therefore I want to retaliate in their favour and ask the hon. gentleman to renew the contract with them. They are a little afraid that the new memJber for Gaspe might influence the hon. gentleman against them; but I hope he is too good-hearted to listen to such advice.

My hon. friend took good care to tie the matter up before he went out, because the contract runs to 1913.
Steam service between St. John and Halifax,

I would like to direct the attention of the minister to the fact, that it is very desirable to have the steamship operated in connection with this service, call at Westport and Freeport, en route for St. John. This wall not take the vessel out of her way, and as the^ subsidy paid, is a very substantial one, it seems to me, there should be a call made at these ports. There is now a service between Westport and St. John, but it is maintained by a comparatively small boat. The trade of the communities at which this boat calls, has increased of late years, and the service now is not sufficient to meet their demands. I was approached, when in Halifax, recently, by some gentlemen who were interested in the operation of this service, and told that they could call at these ports, if they received an increase of $1,000 in the subsidy. I am not prepared to say that any such increase would be warranted, but I do not think it would take the vessel out of its way to call there. I trust that the minister in making any contract with these gentlemen will see his way clear to provide that such a call be made. The business of Westport and Freeport is suffering somewhat for lack of sufficient service. They are altogether out of touch with railways, and the only means of communication is by steamship. I had a letter the other day from a gentleman who is carrying on a very extensive fishing business, and he told me that because of the insufficient steamship service, the business of his firm had been prejudiced. The people of Westport and Freepoit are very anxious indeed that this boat should call, and I cannot urge this matter too strongly upon the minister.

I doubt very
much whether it would be fair to ask the persons who now have the contract, to extend the service without some compensation being granted. I doubt, in fact, if they would be allowed, even with extra payment, to call at Freeport and Westport, because I do not think they could properly perform the service they are now under contract for, namely a weekly service between St. John and Halifax, and call at so many intermediate points.

As a
matter of fact, the contractors are not performing a weekly service. The contract was for 52 trips, but I found that the contract was given them for 40 trips. I do not quite know why that was done. It may have been done from the representation that they found it impossible, from their point of view, to make 52 trips for the subsidy that was offered, and that a compromise was effected, by giving them the contract for 40 trips by the same route. I have not sufficient information on the point, and I do not know quite whether I ought to fix this contract on the same basis as last year or not. I have not looked into the matter sufficiently to tell. However, we can come back to this vote, as we are allowing one item to stand, and I would look into the subject a little more. With reference to the call at Freeport, looking at the map, one would think it was on a direct course, but you cannot always tell that by a mere reference to the map. If it were not to take the vessel off its course -that is, make her voyage longer-it would seem to me, that the contractors might take up the idea of calling at that port, as I am informed, there is good water and good landing. I will say to my hon. friend (Mr. Jameson) that I will take the matter up with the contractors and see whether or not this can be done.
Steamship service between St. John and Halifax or either, and the West Indies and South America, $79,500.
Is there anything new in regard to the West Indies?
No, there is nothing new. To be frank with the committee, the position of matters is just aibout this
I suppose you will discuss the matter with the delegates from the West Indies?

Yes. They will be here about the last of the month, and we will take up with them the steamship service, as well as other matters. At present I would not like to make any change either by dropping the vote or otherwise.
Steam service between Sydney and Wycoco-magli, $3,000.

The minister will find from various petitions and other communications on file in his department, that for many years I have been struggling to have this subsidy increased. The stretch of water from Sydney to Wycocomagh, with which, perhaps, the minister is acquainted, is served entirely by this boat, the steamer ' Marion.' There is no railroad touching places at all on either side of

the lake, and this boat moves on a very zig-zag route, crossing from side to side, and serving the people highly satisfactory in so far as any one boat can do it. The subsidy she receives, I think the minister will hind, is small in proportion to the service she renders that very large tract of country which contains a very large population. I was trying ibefore the present minister assumed charge of the department, to obtain a subsidy of $4,000 a year for this service. Petitions and communications on file would show that, and I really hope that upon ascertaining the service which this vessel has been rendering, the minister will see his way clear to give that necessary and desirable increase.

When
did my hon. friend enter the House?
My first coming here was in 1904.
My hon. friend says he has been struggling and has not accomplished anything.
Not very much.

I see that in 1907, eighty round trips were made and a subsidy of $1,000 was paid. In 1909, 85 trips were made, and the subsidy paid was $2,000. That is 100 per cent increase in the subsidy. In 1911, 78 trips were made and $3,000 was paid in subsidy. Now my hon. friend has been exerting himself and yet did not know that he had accomplished so much in raising the subsidy.
The minister ought to go one better.

I think there is this to be taken into account- that a steamship company ought to consider it a privilege to carry on operations in such a beautiful part of the country. This vessel has had a substantial business in freight and passengers, and I find that business has been all the time increasing in both respects, which is very satisfactory. Last year the vessel carried 6,051 passengers, 1,690 tons of freight, and 4,738 head of live stock, which was a very good increase over preceding years. I am tenderhearted in a way and I will look into the matter and see what can be done.

A subsidy of $1,000 was hardly worth mentioning' in connection with such a service, and the goal of our ambition was that we should get the subsidy for /that very excellent service* increased to $4,000, when we intended to stop worrying the department any further.
I hope that $4,000 will be given.
If my hon. friend makes a threat of worrying too much he may get the $4,000.

If the minister will permit me I would like to return to the item for the service between Guysborough and Mulgrave. This is a daily service starting from the town of Guysborough every morning and connecting * with the train at Mulgrave. In the summer time this vessel carries the mails.
In the winter the mails are carried by coach. This boat calls at Queensport on the way to Mulgrave every morning. But on the return trip, it takes her out of her course a few miles to call at Queensport, and she has been accustomed to make the trip direct. Queensport is the centre for a number of small places. Passengers for Queensport or any of these places are now taken to Guysborough, and remain there all night, going back to Queensport the following morning. Objection is taken by the town of Guysborough, because they want a direct trip from Mulgrave to Guysborough. I took the view that where there were passengers from Mulgrave to Queensport or any place reached from Queensport, the steamer should go the few miles out of her way necessary to land these passengers. Last year instructions to that effect were given to the captain, I believe. It was represented there were not passengers every day, and the compromise I suggested was that when there were passengers, the ship should1 call at Queensport; if not she should make her direct course to Guysborough. I would like the minister to look into that matter, and see if this can be arranged.
I have some complaint from Guysborough.

I would like to give notice that when we go into Supply on some
occasion when the minister can listen to me, I intend to discuss the question of the Canada-France steamship line, and our trade relations with France.
I hope my hon. friend keeps Easter in view. Condense it.

Yes. Always keeping Easter in view, may I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to press some of his colleagues to lay on the table the returns that were asked1 for long ago. I refer especially to the Postmaster General.
Will that make Easter come quicker?

Yes.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FOSTER (North Toronto), moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up on Monday?
The third reading of the Grain Bill, and other government Bills.
Which Bills?

There are two third readings, the Grain Bill, and the Bill to amend the Civil Service Act. The Bill for the Aid and Encouragement of Agriculture stands for second reading, and also the Civil Service Bill relating to the post office. These two Bills will be taken up as well. After that probably estimates.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.22 p.m.
Monday, March 11, 1918.
